q-122424:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-1,{t}^{2}-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-1)\,\text{d}t,\int ({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-t+{C}_{1},\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨10,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨3({3}^{2})-3+{C}_{1},\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-3+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨10,-1⟩ & =⟨24+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-14$ and ${C}_{2}=-7.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-t-14,\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t-7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨3({1}^{2})-1-14,\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}-1-7⟩ \\  & =⟨-12,-\frac{23}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-122471:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},0⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\text{d}t,\int 0\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t}+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1}+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-1.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{t},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t,\int (-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{C}_{3},-t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(1)=⟨2,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨2,3⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=2$ and ${C}_{4}=4.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2+\operatorname{ln}⁡t,4-t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-7221:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-2,4⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,4t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,4⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨3(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,4(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,4⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (3{t}^{2}-2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+{C}_{3},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(1)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}+{C}_{3},\,2(1)^{2}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},2+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=0$ and ${C}_{4}=-2.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2},\,2{t}^{2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-104487:
Since $f(x)$ has roots ${x}_{1}=-5$ and ${x}_{2,3}=\pm 3\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2})(x-{x}_{3}) \\  & =3(x-(-5))(x-3\text{i})(x-(-3\text{i})) \\  & =3(x+5)(x-3\text{i})(x+3\text{i})\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3(x+5)(x-3\text{i})(x+3\text{i}) & = \\ 3(x+5)({x}^{2}-(3\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ 3(x+5)({x}^{2}+9) & = \\ 3({x}^{3}+9x+5{x}^{2}+45) & = \\ 3{x}^{3}+15{x}^{2}+27x+135 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=3{x}^{3}+15{x}^{2}+27x+135.$

q-104500:
Let $f(x)=36{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+4x+1.$ Since $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ is a root of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem $(x+\frac{1}{4})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ 

We find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+\frac{1}{4})$ using synthetic division.

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $36$ | $9$ | $4$ | $1$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-9$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
|  | $36$ | $0$ | $4$ | $0$ |

Thus, $f(x)=(x+\frac{1}{4})(36{x}^{2}+4).$ 

To find the remaining two roots, we solve $36{x}^{2}+4=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}36{x}^{2}+4 & =0 \\ 36{x}^{2} & =-4 \\ {x}^{2} & =-\frac{1}{9} \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{3}\text{i})}^{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=-\frac{1}{4},\,\pm \frac{1}{3}\text{i}.$

q-17409:
Let $f(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-24x+160.$ Since $x=-10$ is a root of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem $(x+10)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ 

We find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+10)$ using synthetic division.

$$
\begin{aligned}\enclose{bottom right}{-10} & 1 & 6 & -24 & 160 \\  &  & -10 & 40 & -160 \\  & 1 & -4 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=(x+10)({x}^{2}-4x+16).$ 

To find the remaining two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}-4x+16=0$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+16 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4+12 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2}+12 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-12 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =(2\sqrt{3}\text{i})^{2} \\ x-2 & =\pm 2\sqrt{3}\text{i} \\ x & =2\pm 2\sqrt{3}\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=-10,\,2\pm 2\sqrt{3}\text{i}.$

q-104514:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=3-\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{3-\text{i}}=3+\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(3-\text{i}+(3+\text{i)})x+(3-\text{i})(3+\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+({3}^{2}-(\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+10 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-6x+10$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x+2 \\  & {x}^{2}-6x+10\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+10x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,2{x}^{2}-12x+20 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{2{x}^{2}-12x+20}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

     

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-6x+10)(x+2).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2=0\,⟹\,x=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=-2,3\pm \text{i}.$

q-104516:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-11x-116.$

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=-5+2\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{-5+2\text{i}}=-5-2\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(-5+2\text{i}+(-5-2\text{i)})x+(-5+2\text{i})(-5-2\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+((-5)^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+29 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}+10x+29$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x-4 \\  & {x}^{2}+10x+29\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-11x-116} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}+10{x}^{2}+29x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,-4{x}^{2}+40x-116 \\  & \,\,\,{-4{x}^{2}+40x-116}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

        

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}+10x+29)(x-4).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4=0\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=4,-5\pm 2\text{i}.$

q-72934:
First, we must group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-4x+16y & =-16 \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+(4{y}^{2}+16y) & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must complete the square for both the $x$ and $y$ terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}-4x)+(4{y}^{2}+16y) & =-16 \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+4({y}^{2}+4y) & =-16 \\ [(x-2)^{2}-4]+4[(y+2)^{2}-4] & =-16 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4+4(y+2)^{2}-16 & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rearrange the equation into the desired form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}-4+4(y+2)^{2}-16 & =-16 \\ (x-2)^{2}+4(y+2)^{2} & =-16+16+4 \\ (x-2)^{2}+4(y+2)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{1} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2>1,$ the length of the major axis is $2\cdot 2=4,$ and the length of the minor axis is $2\cdot 1=2.$

q-71116:
Note that the length of the altitude $ZH$ can be related to the area of $△\,WYZ$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}ZH\cdot WY
$$

So, to find $ZH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{WY}$ and $\overset{\to }{WZ}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{WY} & =y-w \\  & =(i+2j+k)-(2i+3j+2k) \\  & =-i-j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-1,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{WZ} & =z-w \\  & =(i-j+k)-(2i+3j+2k) \\  & =-i-4j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-4,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{WY}\times \overset{\to }{WZ} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =((-1)\cdot (-1)-(-4)\cdot (-1))i-((-1)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot (-1))j+((-1)\cdot (-4)-(-1)\cdot (-1))k \\  & =-3i+3k \\  & =⟨-3,0,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{WY}$ and $\overset{\to }{WZ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{WY}\times \overset{\to }{WZ}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,WYZ$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Let's also compute $WY$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}WY & =|\overset{\to }{WY}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}ZH\cdot WY,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}ZH\cdot WY \\ \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}ZH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ 3\sqrt{2} & =ZH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ ZH & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ ZH & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-128008:
Note that the length of the altitude $RH$ can be related to the area of $△\,PQR$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}RH\cdot PQ
$$

So, to find $RH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =q-p \\  & =(2i+3j+k)-(3i+4k) \\  & =-i+3j-3j \\  & =⟨-1,3,-3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =(3j+k)-(3i+4k) \\  & =-3i+3j-3k \\  & =⟨-3,3,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ}\times \overset{\to }{PR} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(3\cdot (-3)-3\cdot (-3))i-((-1)\cdot (-3)-(-3)\cdot (-3))j+((-1)\cdot 3-(-3)\cdot 3)k \\  & =6j+6k \\  & =⟨0,6,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{PQ}\times \overset{\to }{PR}| \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{6}^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{72} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,PQR$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{6\sqrt{2}}{2}=3\sqrt{2}.
$$

Let's also compute $PQ$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =|\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{19}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}RH\cdot PQ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}RH\cdot PQ \\ 3\sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}RH\cdot \sqrt{19} \\ 6\sqrt{2} & =RH\cdot \sqrt{19} \\ RH & =\frac{6\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{19}} \\ RH & =\frac{6\sqrt{38}}{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-142436:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta , \\ y & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

where we used the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$
